w: What's tested hCG: made by the trophoblasts, it rescues the corpus luteum ("this is the important part... this is what rescues the corpus luteum"), keeps progesterone and estrogen high and LH and FSH low, and is what a pregnancy test measures; the corpus luteum carries the first trimester, then the placenta takes over Lactation: prolactin makes the milk and oxytocin lets it down; during pregnancy progesterone holds prolactin back ("what you should know"); dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin, suckling turns it down, and prolactin inhibits GnRH ("one thing that I want to highlight") Fertilization: ZP3 sets off the acrosomal reaction ("one of those proteins that's really important"), then ZP2, the second meiotic division and the cortical reaction that blocks polyspermy; capacitation has to come first The pregnancy steroids ("the main hormones that I care more about"): estriol is the estrogen of pregnancy; the placenta makes progesterone on its own but needs the fetus's 17,20 desmolase to make estrogen Implantation (trophoblasts, cytotrophoblasts versus syncytiotrophoblasts, decidualization) and the placenta's other hormones: human placental lactogen opposes insulin, and relaxin keeps the uterus quiet Labor: a rising estrogen-to-progesterone ratio, prostaglandins and oxytocin from the posterior pituitary, which also limits bleeding after delivery; and the endocrine basis of contraception Dr. Matthew Madison (PhD, Division of Pulmonary, Allergy and Critical Care Medicine) gave Lecture 17 on Tuesday, November 10, at 2 pm, the hour after his lecture on female reproductive physiology. His deck, "Endocrinology of Pregnancy", follows a pregnancy from start to finish: getting sperm and oocyte together, fertilization, implantation and the placenta, the placenta's hormones, delivery, lactation, and a last slide on controlling fertility. He said the emphasis is on the hormones, not on fetal development. These notes follow the recording and slides. His objectives: describe the events of fertilization; relate the maternal endocrine changes that promote fertilization; relate how the sperm become capable of fertilization; explain how implantation and placentation occur; describe maternal-fetal endocrine communication; and discuss the endocrine basis of contraception. Why the cycle matters: a quick review He opened by tying this lecture to the menstrual cycle: pregnancy shows why the cycle has a follicular phase and a luteal phase. In the follicular phase, the first half of the cycle, the growing follicle makes estradiol, and the endometrium is in its proliferative phase, with a lot of cell division. Ovulation comes at midcycle. In the luteal phase, the ruptured follicle turns into the corpus luteum, "a robust endocrine organ," his slide says, that makes large amounts of progesterone, with estrogen. Progesterone is the key hormone that prepares the endometrium for implantation. In the secretory phase, which is the same as the luteal phase, the endometrium's blood vessels become wider and more defined and glycogen vacuoles form. The glycogen is energy for implantation, for building the placenta and for the developing fetus. Without a pregnancy, the corpus luteum lasts about 14 days after ovulation. Then it regresses into a scar, the corpus albicans; estrogen and progesterone fall abruptly, and the endometrium is shed. Keep that in mind: the first hormone of pregnancy exists to stop it. His review slide adds three more points. Progesterone raises the basal body temperature, which stays up through the luteal phase. Vaginal cornification, a keratinization driven by estradiol, toughens the vaginal lining so it withstands physical stress. And the cervical mucus decides how easily sperm get through: under estradiol it turns watery and elastic around ovulation, and in the luteal phase it becomes thick. The road to fertilization About 250 million sperm are deposited in the vagina, and only about 50 make it to the distal fallopian tube, where fertilization usually happens. Those few are the ones likely to fertilize the oocyte released at ovulation. His slide adds that sperm keep their fertilizing capacity for 24 to 48 hours. Around ovulation, estrogen dominates, and it helps the sperm survive and move in three ways. It buffers the vaginal pH. He said it raises the pH, making the vagina less acidic, which protects the sperm. It decreases the viscosity of the cervical mucus: a more watery mucus that sperm swim through easily. It increases contraction of the myometrium, the thick muscle layer just under the endometrium. Its rhythmic contractions help propel the sperm up toward the tubes. On the oocyte's side, the cilia of the fallopian tube help capture the released oocyte and move it down the tube; his slide adds that contraction of the ampulla helps move the egg too. Three layers around the oocyte Even the sperm that reach the oocyte face three barriers, from the outside in. The expanded cumulus: the granulosa cells that surround the ovulated oocyte and keep nourishing it. He called this outer layer the corona radiata. The zona pellucida: a specialized extracellular matrix, a thick, rigid capsule around the oocyte. The oocyte's own plasma membrane, the oolemma, which the sperm finally merges with. Getting through takes the acrosome, the cap on the sperm's head that is packed with enzymes, hyaluronidases and proteases, that break down the zona pellucida. Many sperm working together first break down the cells of the corona radiata. Histology texts use "corona radiata" for the innermost layer of cumulus cells, the ones touching the zona pellucida. The lecture uses it for the whole cumulus layer. Either way it is the outermost barrier the sperm meets. Fertilization: ZP3, ZP2 and one sperm per egg "One of those proteins that's really important is called ZP3." ZP3 sits on the zona pellucida; his slide calls it a species-specific receptor. When a sperm recognizes and binds ZP3, the binding sets off the acrosomal reaction: the acrosome ruptures and releases its enzymes, which digest a path through the zona pellucida. "So ZP3 stimulates the acrosomal reaction." The acrosome's proteases also cleave the ZP3 layer, so it is shed, and a new layer of proteins is exposed. One of them is ZP2. After the acrosomal reaction, the sperm binds ZP2 instead, because the ZP3 receptors are gone. Binding ZP2, he said, starts two things. The oocyte undergoes its second meiotic division and becomes haploid, right before fertilization. He asked the class when the first division happened: at ovulation. The cortical reaction, also called the zonal reaction: the oocyte releases its cortical granules, and the remaining zona proteins are shed, so no other sperm can bind. That prevents polyspermy, fertilization by more than one sperm. A single sperm fertilizes a single egg. Soon after, the male and female pronuclei fuse, and the result is a zygote. ZP3 First, on reaching the zona pellucida The acrosomal reaction: enzymes digest the zona, and the ZP3 layer is cleaved away ZP2 After the acrosomal reaction, once ZP3 is gone The oocyte's second meiotic division, and the cortical (zonal) reaction that blocks polyspermy He and his slide tie the second meiotic division to ZP2 binding. Textbooks such as Costanzo and Guyton say the oocyte completes it once the sperm enters, as it fuses with the oolemma. Both put it at fertilization, right before the pronuclei fuse, which is what to know. Capacitation: sperm aren't ready on arrival Ejaculated sperm cannot fertilize an ovum right away. They arrive in a dormant state, and capacitation has to happen first. The reason is a safety lock. While sperm are stored in the male tract, they sit among vesicles rich in cholesterol, which keep adding cholesterol to their plasma membrane. That makes the membrane so rigid that the acrosome can't rupture too early. In the female tract, the sperm swim away from those vesicles, and the uterine and tubal fluids wash away the inhibitory factors. His slide lists four changes. Membrane fluidity changes as sterols, such as cholesterol, and glycoproteins are removed from the sperm membrane. Proteins and carbohydrates that would block the egg-binding sites are removed. The membrane potential changes, so calcium can enter the sperm, which makes the acrosomal reaction possible once the sperm binds ZP3. Many proteins are phosphorylated, and hyperactivation begins: the tail's beat changes from wave-like to whip-like. In short, capacitation removes the blocks to binding the oocyte and allows the acrosomal reaction. It is a transient event: it starts as the sperm travel through the uterus and happens mainly in the fallopian tube. That is why, soon after ejaculation, there is a stretch when sperm can't fertilize yet. The fallopian tubes At the distal end of each tube are the fimbriae, finger-like projections that capture the oocyte when the follicle ruptures at midcycle and bring it into the tube. Beating cilia and peristaltic contractions of the tube, a response to estrogen, his slide notes say, move it along. Fertilization most often happens in the distal fallopian tube. Estrogen holds the embryo back, progesterone lets it in Estrogen and progesterone act all through pregnancy, and between fertilization and implantation they pull in opposite directions. Just after midcycle, estrogen is still high, and estrogen promotes contraction and constriction. It constricts the opening of the uterus, where the fallopian tube meets it, which keeps the embryo from entering the uterus too soon. The delay gives the endometrium time to get ready. When progesterone rises, the myometrium relaxes, and the blastocyst can move into the uterus and implant in the rich, well-vascularized lining of the luteal phase. One rule runs through the whole lecture: estrogen contracts, progesterone relaxes. It comes back at labor, when the balance tips toward estrogen. The first week: a timeline Fertilization takes place within 24 hours of ovulation, typically on day 15 or 16 of the cycle. Rapid cell division follows. The blastocyst, about 100 cells, enters the uterine cavity about 4 days after ovulation, and implantation happens 5 to 7 days after ovulation. He stressed that these are ranges: "there's no definitive day." About 8 days after ovulation, the trophoblasts start secreting hCG, which he called the important part of his timeline slide. Within 24 hours of ovulation Fertilization, in the distal fallopian tube About 4 days after ovulation The blastocyst enters the uterine cavity 5 to 7 days after ovulation Implantation About 8 days after ovulation The trophoblasts begin secreting hCG 10 to 11 days after fertilization hCG can be found in urine or blood About 14 days after ovulation When the corpus luteum would regress without hCG About 10 weeks hCG peaks, then declines End of the first trimester The placenta is fully developed and takes over hormone production About 40 weeks after the last menstrual period began Parturition The blastocyst As the zygote divides, it passes through stages with their own names, and he said you don't need them: "I don't really care that you know all the different stages for my stuff... no, you don't have to know it." What matters is that implantation happens at the blastocyst stage. A blastocyst has many cells around a fluid-filled cavity, the blastocoele, and its outer layer is made of trophoblasts. The trophoblasts carry out implantation, and implantation is invasive: the blastocyst doesn't just stick to the wall, it has to "set up shop" and build a placenta to nourish the fetus. Implantation The blastocyst secretes three kinds of substances that help it implant: adhesion molecules, proteases and hormones, chiefly hCG. The uterus meets it halfway. Early pregnancy speeds up the decidualization of the endometrium, which makes it more receptive to the blastocyst. Decidualization is a set of changes: increased vascularity; increased glycogen, stored in vacuoles around the implanting blastocyst; and immune modulation, a local suppression of the immune system so it doesn't recognize the blastocyst as foreign and attack it. The luteal phase had already begun the vascular and glycogen changes; hormones from the blastocyst push them further. His slide puts implantation in three steps. Attachment, or adhesion. Adhesion molecules on the trophoblasts and on the endometrial cells bind the blastocyst firmly to the wall. He named L-selectin as one but said, "I don't care that you know them." The important thing is that attachment signals the trophoblasts to differentiate into two populations: cytotrophoblasts, the nurse cells that nourish the early embryo and give it structure, and syncytiotrophoblasts, the invaders. Invasion. The syncytiotrophoblasts send out long protrusions that secrete proteases, which break down the matrix, so the blastocyst burrows deeper into the endometrial stroma. Blastocyst differentiation. The blastocyst secretes paracrine factors that, along with progesterone, amplify the decidual reaction: the endometrial cells enlarge, accumulate glycogen and become decidual cells, which nourish the embryo until the placenta forms. The syncytiotrophoblasts do three jobs: they are adhesive, invasive and endocrine, making hCG and human placental lactogen. They go on to help form the placenta. Role Nurse cells: nourish the early embryo and give it structure Invasion How Support the developing embryo in its early days Long protrusions that secrete proteases and break down the endometrial matrix Hormones None named hCG and human placental lactogen Later Part of the developing placenta Help form the placenta hCG rescues the corpus luteum Human chorionic gonadotropin, or hCG, is secreted by the trophoblasts about 8 days after ovulation. It "informs" the corpus luteum that fertilization has happened. "This is what rescues the corpus luteum." Without it, about 14 days after ovulation, the corpus luteum would regress into the corpus albicans, and estrogen and progesterone would fall abruptly. With it, the corpus luteum stays active, and under hCG's direction it increases its synthesis of progesterone and estrogen. The effect reaches the pituitary too: LH and FSH release from the mother's anterior pituitary is suppressed. He tied this to the secondary amenorrhea of pregnancy, periods that had started and then stop: the cyclic waves of LH and FSH of a normal cycle are shut down. The goal is progesterone and estrogen kept high and steady, to nourish the developing placenta and fetus. His one-line summary: "hCG prevents the regression of corpus luteum, slows production of LH and FSH." He credited hCG itself with slowing LH and FSH, and his slide says it "exerts negative feedback" on the maternal pituitary. Textbooks such as Costanzo credit the high estrogen and progesterone that hCG keeps flowing. Either way, LH and FSH stay low through pregnancy. hCG is also what a pregnancy test measures: "it's very high, very quickly." His slide notes add that it can be found in urine or blood about 10 to 11 days after fertilization, and that it is highest toward the end of the first trimester, at about 10 weeks, then declines for the rest of pregnancy. Two more points from the slide's notes. hCG can bind, weakly, to the TSH receptor, which can cause a transient gestational hyperthyroidism. Separately, estrogen raises thyroid-binding globulin, or TBG, so total T3 and T4 can double while free T3 and T4 don't rise much. The notes also mark pregnancy as an insulin-resistant, hyperinsulinemic state, which comes back with human placental lactogen. Corpus luteum first, then placenta Rescued by hCG, the corpus luteum stays intact and makes most of the progesterone and estrogen during the first trimester, because the placenta isn't fully formed yet. The placenta begins developing shortly after implantation and is fully developed by the end of the first trimester. After that, it takes over the hormone production. The placenta The placenta has several jobs: Nutrient and gas exchange: oxygen and nutrients in from the mother's blood, carbon dioxide and waste out. Hormone production: hCG, progesterone, estrogen and human placental lactogen. Immune protection: a selective barrier that protects the fetus from many infections while letting maternal antibodies through. Waste removal: fetal waste goes into the mother's circulation, and she excretes it. A regulatory barrier that controls what crosses from mother to fetus, drugs, nutrients and antibodies included. Support for fetal development: growth, organ development and priming of the immune system. Mother to fetus Oxygen, water, electrolytes, nutrients (lipids, amino acids, carbohydrates, vitamins), hormones and antibodies; and some drugs and viruses Fetus to mother Carbon dioxide and other waste products, hormones and antibodies He stressed the downside too: certain drugs and some viruses can pass from mother to fetus, so not everything that crosses is welcome. Most of his focus, though, is the placenta's hormones. Human placental lactogen Besides progesterone and estrogen, the placenta makes what he called accessory hormones, which prepare for life after birth or keep the pregnancy going. Human placental lactogen, or hPL, also called human chorionic somatomammotropin, affects the growth and development of breast tissue. It also has anti-insulin actions: it promotes lipolysis and the breakdown of carbohydrates and proteins, which keeps a continuous flow of nutrients going to the fetus. That is part of why pregnancy is an insulin-resistant, hyperinsulinemic state: the mother's tissues respond less to insulin, she uses more fat and spares glucose, and her insulin levels can run very high. Some mothers develop gestational diabetes. He called it multifactorial. Much of it is hormonal, since several placental and pregnancy hormones oppose insulin, but some women have a higher genetic predisposition, and no single hormone drives it. hPL is the one with research interest. Relaxin Relaxin is made by both the corpus luteum, in response to hCG, and the placenta. It inhibits myometrial contractions, keeping the uterus quiet, or quiescent, in early pregnancy, because "the last thing we want is a preterm delivery." It also relaxes the pelvic bones and ligaments and softens the cervix, and at the end of term it may help relax and thin the cervix for delivery. Making progesterone and estrogen: mother, placenta and fetus "Let's look at the main hormones that I care more about": the estrogens and progesterone. All of them start from cholesterol supplied by the mother, mostly from her diet. Progesterone is simple: the placenta can make it on its own, and after the first trimester it supplies it to both mother and fetus. Estrogen is trickier. The predominant estrogen of pregnancy is estriol. The three estrogens each belong to a stage of life: estradiol is the estrogen of the normal menstrual cycle, estrone the estrogen of menopause, and estriol the estrogen of pregnancy. The placenta has cholesterol desmolase, so it can turn cholesterol into pregnenolone, and it has aromatase, the enzyme that turns androgens into estrogens. But it lacks 17,20 desmolase, and you need an androgen to make an estrogen. The fetus has that enzyme. So the work goes back and forth. The placenta makes pregnenolone from the mother's cholesterol and passes it to the fetus. The fetal adrenal gland, with its 17,20 desmolase, makes the androgen DHEA and adds a sulfate, giving DHEA sulfate. The sulfate keeps the androgen from virilizing the fetus. The fetal liver hydroxylates it, giving 16-hydroxy DHEA sulfate. Back in the placenta, aromatase converts it to estriol. Because estriol needs a working fetal adrenal and liver, the mother's estriol level reflects the health of the fetus. The placenta can also use DHEA sulfate to make estradiol. The take-home, in his slide notes: to make estrogen, the placenta "needs help from the baby." Mother Supplies the cholesterol, mostly from the diet Cholesterol Placenta Cholesterol desmolase Pregnenolone, and progesterone on its own Fetal adrenal 17,20 desmolase, then a sulfate added DHEA sulfate Fetal liver 16-hydroxylation 16-hydroxy DHEA sulfate Placenta Aromatase Estriol Names: the deck's "17,20 desmolase" is what textbooks call 17,20-lyase, part of the CYP17 enzyme; "cholesterol desmolase" is the side-chain cleavage enzyme. His slide notes say the fetal adrenal can start from cholesterol; he described pregnenolone passed over from the placenta. Either way, the fetal adrenal supplies the 17,20 step the placenta lacks. Parturition Parturition is the delivery of the fetus, about 40 weeks after the onset of the last menstrual period; labor can of course come sooner. It takes several signals working together: estrogen, progesterone, oxytocin, prostaglandins and relaxin. Some are well understood; for others the evidence is still accumulating. His slide lists the factors that start labor and keep it going. Distention of the uterus as the fetus grows. He described it as a trigger: the baby gets so large that it pushes on the uterine wall, and the mechanical stretch sets off hormonal signals. Upregulation of uterine receptors for PGF2 alpha and oxytocin. He said PGF2 alpha is really important in the uterus, tied to contraction and delivery. Increased uterine sensitivity to estrogen and decreased sensitivity to progesterone. Estrogen increases uterine contractility and progesterone relaxes the myometrium, so as the ratio of estrogen to progesterone rises late in pregnancy, around 40 weeks, the myometrium shifts to a contracting state. Increased uterine production of prostaglandins, PGE2 and PGF2 alpha. They raise intracellular calcium, and calcium drives muscle contraction, so contractions get stronger and more rhythmic. Prostaglandins also soften and thin the cervix; he singled out PGE2 for the softening. Increased oxytocin secretion from the mother's posterior pituitary, "the big one." He asked the class where oxytocin comes from: the posterior pituitary, one of its two hormones. It is a powerful stimulant of uterine contraction, and it synergizes with the prostaglandins. His slide notes describe the oxytocin loop as positive feedback: the contractions bring more oxytocin, not less, until they are strong enough to deliver the baby. And oxytocin keeps working after delivery. The contractions continue after the placenta is delivered, which prevents excessive bleeding: "oxytocin has a role both during active delivery and post-delivery." Relaxin, from earlier, helps change the cervix's tissue and thin it for delivery. His slide notes also describe animal studies in which the fetus's adrenal axis surges cortisol and shifts the placenta toward estrogen. The human placenta lacks that enzyme, so the human trigger is different and not fully known. He didn't teach this part aloud. Lactation: building the breast during pregnancy The structures for lactation develop during pregnancy, driven by the high estrogen and progesterone made first by the corpus luteum and then by the placenta. Estrogen: ductal and lobular growth and ductal branching, and more fat deposition in the breast. Breast fat expresses aromatase, so it makes estrogen locally. Progesterone: increases the number of alveoli, the milk-producing structures. Prolactin: rises, especially later in pregnancy, and increases the enzymes that produce milk. Cortisol: also increases the milk enzymes. "What you should know is that a lot of prolactin's effects during pregnancy are inhibited. They're kind of antagonized by progesterone." Progesterone antagonizes prolactin, especially locally in the breast, so the high placental progesterone suppresses milk production. There may be a little milk, but full milk production doesn't start until after delivery. The development continues all the same, setting the stage. After delivery: prolactin makes milk, oxytocin lets it down Once the baby and placenta are delivered, progesterone falls, and prolactin's brake comes off. Prolactin then drives full milk production in the alveoli. Around each alveolus are myoepithelial cells, which respond to oxytocin by contracting, and that squeezes the milk out: milk letdown. "Prolactin sets the stage and creates all the milk products. Oxytocin is going to stimulate milk letdown." His shorthand: prolactin, milk production; oxytocin, milk letdown. A question that swaps the two is the obvious trap. How prolactin and oxytocin are controlled Normally, prolactin is tonically inhibited: without a baby to feed, there's no need for milk. The hypothalamus does it by constantly releasing dopamine, "a potent inhibitor of prolactin release from the anterior pituitary." So in most people, prolactin stays low. After delivery the brake is released. Suckling decreases dopamine, and he added that the sounds and sight of the baby and the emotions around delivery can lower it too. With dopamine down, the anterior pituitary releases prolactin, and prolactin releasing factor pushes it up further. Low dopamine means high prolactin. Some prolactin is made during pregnancy, but this whole circuit turns on after the baby is delivered. Suckling also makes the hypothalamus produce oxytocin, which is carried to the posterior pituitary and released into the blood to reach the breast. "One thing that I want to highlight": prolactin inhibits GnRH, gonadotropin-releasing hormone. Less GnRH means less LH and FSH and lower sex steroids downstream, which is why high prolactin brings amenorrhea. It is the same mechanism as hyperprolactinemia, high prolactin from any cause, and it is why a breastfeeding mother's periods often stop. On this slide, he said, "mainly focus on this side of things. Dopamine being important." Suckling Dopamine falls; oxytocin rises Low dopamine, plus prolactin releasing factor High prolactin Prolactin Full milk production; inhibits GnRH, so LH, FSH and the cycle shut down Oxytocin, from the posterior pituitary Myoepithelial cells contract: milk letdown He said a baby's sounds and sight and the emotions of delivery lower dopamine. Physiology texts tie the baby's cry mainly to the oxytocin side, the letdown reflex. No question here depends on which. Controlling fertility "I'm not gonna belabor this," he said, but the endocrine basis of contraception is one of his objectives. His slide sorts the methods three ways. Prevent ovulation Oral contraceptives Their estrogens blunt the LH surge, so there is no normal ovulation; they also thin the uterine lining and thicken the cervical mucus Prevent contact of sperm and egg Abstinence, coitus interruptus, barriers, the IUD He didn't go into these Prevent implantation High doses of estrogen, the IUD, progesterone receptor antagonists The lining lacks progesterone's preparation, so the embryo can't implant The progestin in some pills makes the cervical mucus very thick, so sperm can't get into the uterine cavity. High doses of estrogen prevent implantation: they push the endometrium into a proliferative state but bypass everything progesterone does, so the lining is built up but lacks the receptive environment an embryo needs. Progesterone receptor antagonists block progesterone's effects on the lining directly. Estrogen and progesterone, start to finish At ovulation Dominates: buffers vaginal pH, thins cervical mucus, myometrial contractions move sperm Thick cervical mucus in the luteal phase Between fertilization and implantation Constricts the opening of the uterus, holding the embryo back Relaxes the myometrium, letting the blastocyst in Endometrium Proliferative phase Key hormone preparing it for implantation; amplifies decidualization Made in pregnancy by Corpus luteum, then placenta with the fetus's help (estriol) Corpus luteum, then placenta on its own Near term Ratio rises: contraction Uterus less sensitive to it Breast in pregnancy Ducts, branching, fat More alveoli; antagonizes prolactin Contraception In the pill: blunts the LH surge; high doses prevent implantation Progestin thickens mucus; receptor antagonists prevent implantation
